title: Human capital is produced across homes, neighborhoods, and workplaces, so location, care, safety, and job quality shape lifetime opportunity
source_unit: World Bank Group Human Capital Report 2026, Building Human Capital Where It Matters: Homes, Neighborhoods, and Workplaces, with Human Capital Index Plus 2026 findings brief
geography: Global; HCI+ country and regional comparisons, with detailed evidence from low- and middle-income countries and country examples

denominator.unit: low- and middle-income countries assessed for changes in nutrition, learning, or workforce skill development

countries_with_decline.unit: countries experiencing a decline in at least one of nutrition, learning, or workforce skill development

future_earnings_loss_lmic.unit: percent of future labor earnings estimated to be lost in low- and middle-income countries due to current health, education, and work-skill deficits

global_future_earnings_gap.unit: percent of potential future earnings the average child born today could gain if human capital matched top performers at similar income levels

mechanism.value: Human-capital stagnation is not only a school problem; it is an accumulation failure across early care, local environments, and the transition into productive work

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of global human-capital trends and the HCI+ index, which integrates health, education, and employment dimensions through age 65.
observations.uncertainty: The HCI+ is a modeled comparative index and the future-earnings translation is an interpretation of gaps, not a forecast of individual earnings or a causal estimate of any single intervention.
observations.subgroup: Children and working-age populations globally, with particular attention to low- and middle-income countries and regional income bands.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income, institutions, labor demand, migration, health, and measurement quality also shape earnings; the index cannot attribute every gap to human-capital policy alone.

observations.period: Childhood through adolescence; home setting and early skill formation

denominator.unit: World Bank cross-country evidence synthesis on home environments and child development

maternal_education_gradient.value: Children whose mothers have more education perform better on vocabulary and mathematics tests, with gaps remaining broadly constant through childhood and adolescence

care_environment.value: Resources alone do not always compensate for low levels of care; nurturing, reading, play, emotional support, and safety shape development

program_earnings_association.value: Evidence summarized by the report indicates that effective early-childhood and parenting programs can improve adult earnings by nearly 40 percent
program_earnings_association.unit: reported long-run estimate from cited evidence

mechanism.value: Household time, resources, care quality, and parental capability transmit advantage before formal schooling and can compound across generations

observations.method: World Bank evidence review on human-capital accumulation at home, including parental education, care environments, and early-childhood interventions.
observations.uncertainty: The report synthesizes evidence from multiple studies and settings; the cited earnings estimate should not be treated as a universal treatment effect or a guarantee from any single parenting program.
observations.subgroup: Children and adolescents, parents and caregivers, girls and boys, and families with different education, resources, care environments, and exposure to violence.
observations.counterinterpretation: Schools, peers, health, genetics, neighborhood conditions, and labor markets also contribute; home support may be partly a marker for broader family and institutional resources.

observations.period: Across the life course; neighborhood exposure and intergenerational opportunity

denominator.unit: World Bank comparative neighborhood and human-capital evidence frame

brazil_neighborhood_earnings.value: In a cited Brazil example, a low-income child growing up in a low-income neighborhood earns half as much as a low-income child growing up in a high-income neighborhood

service_and_safety_route.value: Neighborhoods shape access to schools, health care, safe streets, jobs, pollution exposure, crime, and infrastructure

same_income_different_outcomes.value: Families with the same income can experience substantially different human-capital outcomes depending on where they live

mechanism.value: Place converts household resources into different opportunity sets through service quality, safety, pollution, transport, peer environments, and access to jobs

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of neighborhood effects, service access, environmental exposure, and place-based human-capital evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The report uses cited place-based evidence and examples rather than a single universal neighborhood causal estimate; residential selection and unmeasured family factors remain relevant.
observations.subgroup: Low-income children and families across neighborhoods with different service quality, safety, environmental exposure, transport, and labor-market access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Families may sort into neighborhoods based on resources, preferences, social networks, or risk, so observed place differences are not automatically caused by neighborhood conditions alone.

observations.period: Working life; workplace learning and job quality in low- and middle-income countries

denominator.unit: World Bank evidence synthesis on workers and firms in low- and middle-income countries

limited_learning_work.unit: percent of workers in low- and middle-income countries estimated to be in small-scale agriculture, low-quality self-employment, or micro firms

experience_earnings_gap.value: For the same gain in experience, earnings of self-employed workers increase only about half as much as earnings of salaried workers

women_participation_route.value: Childcare and safe commuting are identified as workplace-adjacent investments that can increase women’s labor-force participation and skill accumulation

mechanism.value: A job can either compound human capital through training and experience or trap workers in low-learning, low-productivity work; labor-market institutions and surrounding care infrastructure affect which path occurs

observations.method: World Bank comparative labor-market and human-capital synthesis, with workplace learning and employment-status comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The reported share and earnings comparison summarize heterogeneous labor markets and do not establish that formal employment or childcare alone causes the observed productivity difference.
observations.subgroup: Workers in low- and middle-income countries, including self-employed workers, salaried workers, women facing care and commuting barriers, and youth entering the labor market.
observations.counterinterpretation: Self-employment can offer autonomy, flexibility, or entrepreneurial upside not captured by average earnings growth; formal jobs can also be low-quality or offer limited learning.

denominator.unit: World Bank HCI+ country comparison and gender decomposition

female_male_hci_gap.unit: HCI+ points lower for the female population than the male population, with the gap largely explained by labor-force participation and job quality

income_comparable_variation.value: Countries with similar income levels often achieve very different HCI+ scores, with an average 90th–10th percentile gap of about 60 points within income bands

top_performers.value: Jamaica, Kenya, Kyrgyz Republic, and Viet Nam are highlighted as strong performers for their income levels

mechanism.value: Institutions, gender norms, job quality, care infrastructure, and policy choices can turn similar national resources into different human-capital trajectories

observations.method: World Bank HCI+ index decomposition and income-band benchmarking across countries, health, education, and employment dimensions.
observations.uncertainty: Index comparisons depend on component definitions, weights, missingness, and cross-country comparability; a gender gap in the index is not a standalone causal estimate of discrimination or any specific policy effect.
observations.subgroup: Female and male populations, countries at similar income levels, and children whose future human capital is projected through age 65.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower female HCI+ score can reflect labor-force participation, job quality, health, education, or measurement differences; country rankings should not be read as fixed national traits.

related_sources.claim: Interactive HCI+ data and country comparisons accompanying the report.
World Bank reproducibility package for the flagship report.

boundary: This record adds a comparative human-capital route from home care and resources through neighborhood exposure, services, workplace learning, gendered labor participation, job quality, and future earnings. It synthesizes World Bank evidence and HCI+ modeled comparisons; it is not respondent-level analysis, a causal evaluation of a single program, a complete measure of wellbeing, or a claim that human capital is reducible to earnings.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank Human Capital Report 2026 page, press release, HCI+ findings brief, and reproducibility metadata reviewed for global deficits, home care, neighborhood effects, workplace learning, gender decomposition, income-band comparisons, and index boundaries.
